posts.title: ‘The Turning Tide’ is retired admiral’s latest foray into fiction
posts.description: Over the course of his 37 years in the military and beyond, Adm. (ret.) James Stavridis has become well-known for many things: his service as Supreme Allied Commander at NATO; his appearances on CNN, where he breaks down the news as senior military analyst; being sanctioned by the Kremlin for his opposition to Vladimir Putin; and as a “New York Times” bestselling author, a designation he earned with the release of “ 2034 ,” a geopolitical military thriller imagining the fallout from a global war with China. Stavridis’ latest novel, “The Turning Tide,” explores the complex realities of World War II through the eyes of hero Scott Bradley James, a young sailor amidst the maelstrom of the era’s significant events: Iwo Jima to Okinawa and the United States’ use of the atomic bomb. The novel is Stavridis’ latest exploration, too, of the myriad ways leadership shapes the course of history. “I’ve always been a writer,” Stavridis said in an interview with Military Families Magazine . posts.title: Navy veteran creates free Space-A travel tool for adventurous military families
posts.description: What started as a retired sailor’s hobby project has turned into a resource to help military families navigate Space-A travel. John Coker, affectionately known as “Pops,” created the app he needed, sharing that emergency open-heart surgery in January 2025 “woke him up.” His new focus? To travel and enjoy life. When creating Pop’s Flight Finder in the Spring of 2026, he hoped to help other military families do just that. Space-Available, commonly known as Space-A, is a benefit for military members and their families to travel using non-commercial military flights. It offers Department of War (DOW) or Air Mobility Command (AMC) aircraft at a free or reduced cost. While these aircraft typically carry supplies and service members, the remaining space is sometimes filled with eligible travelers. posts.title: Program helps junior enlisted military members travel home in exchange for volunteer hours
posts.description: A military-focused nonprofit is closing the distance gap between active-duty service members and their loved ones while encouraging volunteerism. Miles for Military , a Boston-based charity, provides free flights home for active-duty E1s through E4s in exchange for giving back: each flyer must first prove they have completed 25+ verified volunteer hours with a certified nonprofit, on-base organization or other approved community organization. That way, troops get to go home while communities are strengthened — not to mention the relationship between the two deepens. “People often tell me, ‘This has got to be a scam; there’s got to be a catch,’ but I’m like, ‘No, you’ve just got to go!’” said Sgt. Dakota Barnes, a California Army reservist who became the nonprofit’s first flyer out of Fort Bragg, North Carolina in 2024, when she was active duty. “Miles for Military is a community within a community, that builds community, that facilitates more community.
